title: Computer architecture
summary: x86, Arm and RISC-V compared; instruction encoding, pipelines, Amdahl's law and the memory hierarchy.

learn.plain: Think of an instruction set as a language and a chip as someone who speaks it. x86, Arm and RISC-V are three languages. Software written in one runs on any chip that speaks it, whether that chip is fast or slow. Pipelining is an assembly line: while one instruction is being finished, the next ones are already being started.
learn.engineer: High-performance cores decode 6 to 10 instructions per cycle into micro-operations, rename registers to remove false dependencies, and execute out of order from windows of several hundred instructions behind branch predictors that are right well over 95% of the time. x86 pays a decode cost for variable-length instructions, usually hidden by a micro-op cache; fixed-length Arm and RISC-V decode in parallel more easily. Today the ISA matters less for raw speed than for ecosystem, licensing and extensions such as Arm SME, RISC-V vector and matrix extensions, and x86 AVX10 and AMX.

quiz.q: What does an instruction set architecture (ISA) define?
options: The exact transistor layout of a chip
The instructions software can use and how each is encoded in bits
The clock speed of the processor
quiz.why: The ISA is the contract between software and hardware. Many different chips can implement the same ISA.

quiz.q: Which statement about RISC-V is true?
options: Only Intel and AMD may build it
Every chip pays a royalty to use it
It is an open standard anyone can implement royalty-free
Its instructions are 1 to 15 bytes long
quiz.why: RISC-V is run by RISC-V International and is free to implement. Arm charges royalties; x86 is limited to Intel and AMD.

quiz.q: Why do GPUs beat CPUs at AI math, according to Amdahl's law?
options: Each GPU core is faster than a CPU core
AI matrix math is almost entirely parallel, so thousands of simple lanes win
GPUs run at higher clock speeds
quiz.why: When 99.9% of the work can run in parallel, the serial part barely matters and massive parallelism wins.
